title: Applied anatomy: the spleen and elective splenectomy

guidelineVersions: UKHSA Green Book chapter 7 (January 2020) and chapter 25 (29 July 2026)

brief.scenario: Chloe Henderson, 28, has hereditary spherocytosis and is listed for elective laparoscopic splenectomy.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the anatomy of the spleen, the structures at risk at splenectomy, and how you would protect her from infection afterwards.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Position, relations, ligaments and vessels, then what surgery puts at risk, then lifelong infection risk.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Stopping at vaccines. She also needs antibiotics, a card, and a plan if she gets a fever.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant, posteriorly, under the lower left ribs."

grid.label: Position and relations
grid.fail: Places the spleen anteriorly, or cannot name its relations.
grid.pass: Posterior left upper quadrant under the lower ribs, against the diaphragm. Relations: stomach, left kidney, splenic flexure, tail of pancreas at the hilum.
grid.high: Links surfaces to relations (diaphragmatic, gastric, renal, colic) and notes lower left rib fractures should raise suspicion of splenic injury.

grid.label: Ligaments and blood supply
grid.fail: Says the splenic artery comes from the superior mesenteric artery.
grid.pass: Splenic artery from the coeliac trunk along the upper pancreas; splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
grid.high: Gastrosplenic ligament carries short gastric vessels; splenorenal ligament carries splenic vessels and pancreatic tail. Both derive from dorsal mesogastrium.

grid.label: Structures at risk
grid.fail: Cannot name a structure injured at splenectomy.
grid.pass: Tail of pancreas, greater curvature of stomach with short gastric vessels, splenic flexure of colon, diaphragm, splenic vessels.
grid.high: Pancreatic tail injury causes a fistula or collection; searches for accessory spleens, which can cause relapse of haemolysis if missed.

grid.label: Vaccination
grid.fail: Omits vaccination, or lists only pneumococcal.
grid.pass: Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY, meningococcal B, and annual influenza. Hib is no longer needed for adults.
grid.high: Adult schedule: one pneumococcal dose repeated every 5 years; one MenACWY; two MenB doses 4 weeks apart.

grid.label: Timing
grid.fail: Vaccinates on the morning of surgery, or delays a needed splenectomy to vaccinate.
grid.pass: Ideally 4 to 6 weeks before elective splenectomy, at least 2 weeks before. If not possible, at least 2 weeks after.
grid.high: Gives the reason: antibody responses are better 2 weeks after surgery. Never delays an emergency splenectomy for vaccines.

grid.label: Antibiotic prophylaxis
grid.pass: Daily prophylaxis, usually phenoxymethylpenicillin (a macrolide if allergic), essential in the first years and often continued lifelong.
grid.high: Adds a standby course at home for fever, and prompt treatment of animal bites.

grid.label: Patient education
grid.fail: Does not warn her about overwhelming infection.
grid.pass: Explains lifelong risk of overwhelming infection, and gives the splenectomy card to carry.
grid.high: Tells her to seek help the same day for fever, and to get travel advice, including malaria precautions.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Where is the spleen and what are its relations?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: In the left upper quadrant, just under the anterior abdominal wall, next to the liver.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Where does the splenic artery come from?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What could you injure during the operation?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'm not sure. Mainly the spleen itself, if it bleeds.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How will you protect her from infection afterwards?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She needs a pneumococcal vaccine. We can give it on the morning of surgery.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, once she's vaccinated she's protected.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Posteriorly in the left upper quadrant, under the lower left ribs, against the diaphragm. It touches the stomach, the left kidney and the splenic flexure, and the tail of the pancreas reaches the hilum.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The splenic artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk, runs along the upper border of the pancreas. The splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreas to form the portal vein.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is at risk at splenectomy?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The tail of the pancreas, the stomach and short gastric vessels, the splenic flexure, the diaphragm and the splenic vessels.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Pneumococcal, meningococcal ACWY and B, and annual influenza. Hib isn't needed now for adults.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Ideally 4 to 6 weeks before surgery and at least 2 weeks before. If that can't happen, at least 2 weeks after.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Daily antibiotic prophylaxis, usually phenoxymethylpenicillin, or a macrolide if she's allergic. It's essential for the first years and often lifelong. I'd explain the risk of overwhelming infection and give her the splenectomy card.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Describe the surfaces of the spleen.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: It has diaphragmatic, gastric, renal and colic surfaces, matching its relations. It lies under the lower left ribs, so fractures there should make me think of splenic injury.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastrics; the splenorenal ligament carries the splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail. Both come from the dorsal mesogastrium.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Why does the pancreas matter here?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The tail lies in the splenorenal ligament at the hilum. If I injure it, she can get a pancreatic fistula or collection. In spherocytosis I'd also look for accessory spleens, because a missed one can cause haemolysis to recur.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: One pneumococcal dose, repeated every 5 years; one MenACWY; two MenB doses 4 weeks apart; and flu each year.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: If she had needed an emergency splenectomy?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I wouldn't delay surgery. I'd vaccinate at least 2 weeks afterwards, when antibody responses are better.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: What else will you give her?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Daily prophylaxis plus a standby course at home in case she gets a fever. Animal bites need prompt treatment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd tell her to seek help the same day for any fever, carry her card, and get travel advice before going abroad, including malaria precautions.

failures.consequence: Vaccines do not cover all strains; without antibiotics and a fever plan she remains at risk of overwhelming sepsis.

failures.move: Vaccinating on the morning of surgery.
failures.consequence: Too late for a good response; the guidance is at least 2 weeks before, or 2 weeks after.

failures.move: Not naming the tail of the pancreas.
failures.consequence: Misses the injury behind a postoperative fistula or collection.

failures.move: Placing the splenic artery on the superior mesenteric artery.
failures.consequence: Cannot plan vascular control at the hilum.

recovery.line: The organisms are encapsulated: pneumococcus, meningococcus, plus annual flu.
Surgery first; vaccinate at least 2 weeks later.

knowledge.fact: Splenic artery: coeliac trunk. Splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein.
Splenorenal ligament: splenic vessels and pancreatic tail. Gastrosplenic ligament: short gastric vessels.
Hib is no longer recommended for older children and adults with asplenia.
PCV20 is replacing PPV23 for at-risk groups from 2026; asplenic patients are re-immunised every 5 years.
Elective splenectomy: vaccinate 4 to 6 weeks before, at least 2 weeks before; otherwise at least 2 weeks after.
Antibiotic prophylaxis, usually phenoxymethylpenicillin, is advised for asplenic patients.

recall.think: Overwhelming infection after splenectomy; pancreatic tail injury at surgery.
recall.say: "Vaccines, antibiotics, card and a fever plan."
do: Splenectomy card and same-day review for fever

numbers.meaning: ideal vaccine lead time before elective splenectomy; at least 2 weeks

recall.trap: Vaccination alone does not protect against all strains.
recall.finish: Vaccinate, prophylactic antibiotics, card, education; search for accessory spleens at surgery.

partner.opening: Tell me where the spleen lies and what it touches.

reveals.finding: Ask: which structure reaches the hilum of the spleen, and in which ligament does it lie?
Routine childhood vaccines only. No previous pneumococcal or MenB.
Penicillin allergy: urticarial rash as a child.

push.question: Where does the splenic artery come from?
push.expect: Coeliac trunk, along the upper border of the pancreas.

push.question: What can you injure during splenectomy?
push.expect: Pancreatic tail, stomach and short gastrics, splenic flexure, diaphragm.

push.question: Which vaccines?
push.expect: Pneumococcal, MenACWY, MenB, annual flu; no Hib for adults.

push.question: When?
push.expect: 4 to 6 weeks before, at least 2 weeks; otherwise at least 2 weeks after.

push.question: Is vaccination enough?
push.expect: No: daily prophylaxis, standby course, card, fever plan.

curveballs.prompt: Her operation date is in 10 days.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Under 2 weeks is too late for a good response. Do not vaccinate on the day; proceed and vaccinate at least 2 weeks after surgery.
Use a macrolide such as erythromycin for prophylaxis.

curveballs.prompt: Two years later her haemolysis returns.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider a missed accessory spleen; image to look for it.
